item.title: German wholesale prices continue to push higher in September, keeping inflation risks in focus
item.description:
• Germany September wholesale prices +1.9% m/m
  • Prior +0.9%
  • Germany September wholesale prices +8.7% y/y
  • Prior +6.8%

The annual estimate indicates that German wholesale prices are 8.7% higher in September this year compared to the same month a year ago. That marks the highest annual price jump since February 2023 and will add to inflation concerns in the German economy.

Much of the price jump this year can be attributed to the Middle East conflict, which resulted in higher wholesale prices of energy products and intermediate goods such as metals, in particular.

Looking at the details, the main cause of the annual increase in wholesale prices is tied to the increase in the prices of mineral oil products, with prices up 48.8% from September 2025. Compared with August 2026, prices rose by 10.5%.

Meanwhile, the increase in prices in the wholesale of non-ferrous ores, non-ferrous metals and non-ferrous semi-finished metal products (+24.9% on September 2025, +2.1% on August 2026) also had a considerable impact on the development of prices compared with the same month of the previous year.

Overall, the latest reading here continues to paint a rather uncomfortable picture for Germany as businesses continue to face rising input costs. And with energy prices being a major contributor, there is only so much that firms can do to absorb those increases before passing some of the burden on to consumers.

Of course, higher wholesale prices don't necessarily mean that consumer inflation will follow suit immediately. But the longer that these cost pressures persist, the harder it becomes for businesses to shield households from higher prices. And that won't make the ECB's job any easier, especially if higher energy inflation stands feeding through to the broader economy and raising the risks of second-round effects.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Chart of the day: Gold price faces crucial $4,200 breakout test as US CPI looms
item.description:
The $4,200 mark has been a key battleground for gold in the past two weeks, and it could once again be part of the trading action today. The precious metal will face up against a big test from the US CPI report, with the inflation numbers having the potential to draw a broader market reaction that could impact gold.

While there are watchful eyes on the figure level, there's a little more to the technical picture than just that.

Looking at the hourly chart:

Gold's advance from Friday last week has stalled around the $4,200 to $4,220 region before steadying itself closer to $4,150-60 levels in the latest pullback. That coincides with the 100-hour (red line) and 200-hour (blue line) moving averages, which are now converging around the same area. And for now, buyers have at least managed to put up a bit of a fight here.

The bigger challenge though remains getting back above $4,200 and sustaining a break beyond that. The $4,220 region will be another hurdle before buyers can even contemplate chasing the next leg higher in gold.

And that is where the US CPI report later today could come into play. A softer-than-expected core inflation reading could offer gold some relief, particularly if Treasury yields and the dollar fall in response to that.

Having said that, a brief spike above $4,200 isn't exactly going to be convincing enough, at least to me, to signal that the tide has turned.

The daily chart paints a more cautious picture in that regard. The $4,200-20 region will be the first key hurdle and in getting past that, gold buyers will at least see the chart turn to be more constructive. But the next hurdle isn't that far away, with the 100-day moving average (red line) at $4,249 adding another layer of resistance.

On the flip side, a fall back in gold below $4,150 will then put the focus on the region around $4,100-17 closer to the 78.6 Fib retracement level. A break of that will potentially free up the path for the precious metal to dive lower towards $4,000 next.

Looking to the US CPI report later today, it will be more than just the reaction to the initial price spike on the inflation numbers. For gold, it is whether buyers can actually hold on to any gains and reclaim those overhead levels. Otherwise, we'll be back to talking about the same battleground again in the aftermath or perhaps even debate about how another failed push higher could leave gold vulnerable to a deeper retreat.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Economic data spotlight: Will the US CPI report change the Fed's rate hike plans?
item.description:
There's a lot riding on the US CPI report later today, especially with Treasury yields having threatened multi-decade highs over the past week. Going into the report, the consensus is that headline inflation is going to look rather ugly. The question now though is whether markets will actually care all that much.

Headline inflation is expected to rise by 0.6% on the month, taking the annual estimate to 3.6%. It is anticipated that much of the rise will be driven by higher gasoline prices amid the ongoing tensions in the Middle East. Looking to core inflation, that is expected to rise by a more modest 0.2% on the month and 2.5% annually.

Now, the Fed can arguably afford to look past a temporary spike in energy prices. And that is something I would expect policymakers to do in reacting to this report. But if those price pressures start filtering through to other parts of the economy, that is where the story starts becoming something different altogether.

As such, the main focus should really be on core prices today - alongside the details such as shelter costs and services inflation. A surprise there would suggest that underlying price pressures are proving stickier than the Fed might like.

As for the bond market, the reaction there could be telling for how broader markets might react to the inflation numbers.

A hotter headline figure accompanied by a relatively benign core reading might actually give Treasury yields some room to retreat. After all, the market has already been preparing for an ugly headline print as mentioned above.

At this stage, I would argue that it would take a significant upside surprise in core inflation to really send yields surging again. The short-end of the curve is not likely to see much action unless traders become convinced that any inflation surprise warrants a reassessment of the Fed outlook.

Now, could that put an October rate hike back on the table? Possibly, but I reckon that's a really tall order. Fed funds futures are showing just roughly 22% odds of traders expecting the Fed to hike again this month. That's a rather slim chance, especially with higher borrowing costs already doing some of the Fed's tightening work.

As such, it would probably take a genuine shock in core inflation to change that thinking. Otherwise, December remains the more plausible timeline for the next rate hike with traders pricing in roughly 88% odds already of a move.

Taking that into consideration, I would say that we shouldn't be all too surprised if the headline number looks bad but bonds decide to rally anyway in the aftermath of the report. But even then, such a move is likely just traders sensing some short-term relief after all the pressure over the past few weeks.

What matters today isn't necessarily how hot inflation looks at first glance, but whether the underlying details give the Fed another reason to act sooner rather than later. So, that could be what markets choose to focus on in terms of reacting to the inflation numbers this week.

But in the bigger picture, the narrative hasn't exactly changed for the bond market and for broader markets in general. The US-Iran war is still ongoing and keeping energy prices elevated. Fiscal concerns are still very much present and will not be going away any time soon. And inflation pressures are slowly making their way into the broader economy, so that is not allowing for the Fed and other major central banks to rest on their laurels.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: China factory inflation hits 5%, fastest in over four years, as CPI lags at 0.9%
item.description:
The gap between surging factory prices and subdued consumer inflation points to an oil-driven cost shock, not demand-led inflation. That makes crude and commodity prices the main driver of China’s price data for now. China moving from exporting disinflation to passing on higher costs adds to global goods-price pressure, which is unwelcome for central banks already worried about energy-driven inflation, including the Fed and ECB. Margins are the risk at home: manufacturers facing steep input costs but limited pricing power at the consumer end could see profits squeezed. Soft core inflation keeps room for further Chinese policy support, but the PPI jump complicates the case for aggressive easing. The muted equity reaction suggests investors see little near-term policy change from the data.

---

Imported oil costs are pushing China’s factory prices to multi-year highs, but households are not feeling, or paying, the same heat.

Summary:

  • China’s producer price index rose 5% y/y in September, up from 3.8% in August and above the 4.5% expected, the fastest since June 2022; it rose 1.2% m/m from 0.4%
  • Consumer prices rose 0.9% y/y, up from 0.8% but below the 1% forecast, and 0.2% m/m against 0.3% expected
  • Core inflation, excluding food and energy, held at 1%
  • Gasoline prices rose almost 17% y/y, contributing almost half a percentage point to headline CPI
  • Economists said Middle East supply disruption drove sharp increases in fuel processing, chemicals and non-ferrous metals, while weak domestic demand limited pass-through to consumers

China’s factory-gate inflation accelerated to its fastest pace in more than four years in September as higher oil and commodity prices lifted costs for manufacturers, while consumer inflation edged up only modestly amid weak domestic demand.

The producer price index rose 5% from a year earlier, the National Bureau of Statistics said on Wednesday, up from 3.8% in August and above the 4.5% expected. It was the fastest pace since June 2022. On a monthly basis, producer prices jumped 1.2%, compared with 0.4% in August.

Economists said much of the pressure came from commodity supply disruptions linked to the Middle East conflict, with particularly sharp increases in fuel processing, chemicals and non-ferrous metals. Transport disruptions, adverse weather and geopolitical tensions have all added to costs.

Consumer prices rose 0.9% year on year, edging up from 0.8% in August but short of the 1% forecast. Monthly, the CPI gained 0.2%, below expectations of 0.3% and slower than August’s 0.4%. Gasoline prices rose almost 17% from a year earlier and contributed almost half a percentage point to headline inflation, the statistics bureau said.

Underlying price pressures remained muted. Core inflation, which strips out food and energy, was steady at 1%, suggesting households remain cautious about spending. The data underline an uneven recovery that relies more on exports than domestic consumption, with private-sector confidence fragile despite a series of stimulus measures.

That widening gap between producer and consumer prices leaves manufacturers absorbing higher input costs that they struggle to pass on. Economists said a key question is whether stronger industrial activity can eventually feed through into jobs, incomes and consumer confidence, which would help narrow the divergence from the demand side and support a more balanced recovery in 2027. Some expect producer prices to fall back next year as commodity pressures ease.

Beijing has stepped up support, approving an additional 550 billion yuan (around $82 billion) in unused local government bond quota for infrastructure and other spending, adding to measures such as mortgage subsidies.

Chinese markets were little softer after the release. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Lagarde: no second-round effects yet, but ECB can’t wait until they are in full view
item.description:
Lagarde’s message leans hawkish at the margin. A central bank that will act on early hints, without waiting for clear evidence of second-round effects, could move sooner than markets expect if wage settlements firm. That supports front-end European yields and the euro on a relative basis. Energy is the key transmission channel. With inflation driven mainly by energy prices, a further jump in oil or gas from Gulf escalation would raise the odds of pre-emptive tightening, making crude and TTF gas direct inputs into ECB pricing. Her comments on France offer no backstop signal, so the French-German yield spread remains exposed to Paris’s budget politics.

-

Lagarde sees no wage-price spiral yet, but she has made clear the ECB will act on the first signs rather than wait for proof.

Summary:

  • ECB President Christine Lagarde said inflation has been rising predominantly, but not exclusively, because of energy prices
  • She said there are no second-round effects yet, but the ECB cannot wait until they are in full view and will look for early hints
  • The ECB is monitoring wage expectations embedded in collective bargaining agreements as an early warning sign
  • Asked about French debt, Lagarde said the primary solution lies in French fiscal policy
  • She described euro area growth of 1.1% in 2026 as not brilliant but not bad, and said she will not run for French president

European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde said the euro area has yet to see second-round effects from higher energy prices, but signalled the central bank would not wait for them to become fully visible before responding.

Lagarde said inflation has been rising predominantly, though not exclusively, as a result of energy prices. While there is no sign yet of those increases feeding through into broader wages and prices, she said policymakers must anticipate and look for early hints. The ECB is paying particular attention to collective bargaining arrangements, where expectations of future wage increases tend to show up first.

Second-round effects occur when an initial price shock, such as a jump in energy costs, prompts workers to seek higher wages and companies to raise prices further, turning a temporary spike into more persistent inflation. Lagarde’s emphasis on acting before those effects are fully evident suggests a readiness to respond pre-emptively if wage settlements begin to firm.

On the economy, Lagarde said growth is not brilliant, but that euro area growth of 1.1% in 2026 is not bad.

Asked about France’s debt, she said the primary and first solution lies in French fiscal policy. The remark puts the onus on Paris rather than the ECB as French borrowing costs face pressure. Goldman Sachs noted in a recent client discussion that the spread between French and German government bond yields has widened sharply amid political tensions over the French budget, an issue it expects to persist ahead of the French presidential election in the first half of next year.

Lagarde, who is French, also said she will not run for president of France.

Her comments leave energy prices and wage negotiations as the key indicators for the ECB’s next steps. A renewed rise in energy costs, or early evidence of stronger pay demands, would increase pressure on policymakers to act before inflation becomes entrenched. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Goldman Sachs says RBA minutes lower bar for November hike, with three hawkish signals
item.description:
Goldman’s read raises the risk that the next RBA move comes sooner than its own base case. That leaves the third-quarter CPI release as the main event for the Australian dollar and short-dated bond yields. The minutes’ emphasis on domestic capacity shifts the focus from energy pass-through to underlying inflation, so even a moderate headline print could carry hawkish weight if services and core measures stay firm. Oil still matters at the margin: the minutes noted that domestic fuel prices were running well above the RBA’s August assumptions, and a renewed jump in crude tied to the Iran war would strengthen the case for tightening. Market pricing had already leaned toward further hikes before the September decision, so a hot CPI reading could quickly firm up expectations for November.

---

Goldman isn’t calling a November hike yet, but it thinks the RBA minutes have opened the door, and the CPI report later this month will decide whether the board walks through it.

Summary:

  • Goldman Sachs economists said minutes of the RBA’s September meeting were more hawkish than the press conference that followed the decision, citing three reasons
  • Among them, the minutes showed increased concern about domestic capacity pressures, with July’s stronger-than-expected CPI data seen as evidence of that
  • Goldman still expects the RBA to keep the cash rate at 4.60% in November, but says the minutes have lowered the bar for another hike, conditional on third-quarter CPI
  • The minutes showed the board judged excess demand to be greater than previously assessed and said it would raise rates further if required
  • Third-quarter CPI data are due on 28 October, ahead of the RBA’s 2 to 3 November meeting

Minutes of the Reserve Bank of Australia’s September policy meeting have likely lowered the bar for another interest rate increase in November, according to Goldman Sachs economists. The bank still expects rates to stay on hold.

In a report, three members of Goldman’s economics research team said they viewed the minutes, released on Tuesday, as more hawkish than Governor Michele Bullock’s press conference after the decision, for three reasons. Among them, the economists said the minutes showed increased concern about domestic capacity pressures, with the board treating July’s stronger-than-expected inflation data as evidence of that.

Goldman continues to expect the RBA to hold the cash rate at 4.60% at its next meeting. However, it judged that the minutes have lowered the threshold for a further hike in November, depending on the outcome of the third-quarter consumer price index report.

The minutes support that reading. They showed the board unanimously raised rates by 25 basis points at the 28 to 29 September meeting because several upside risks to inflation flagged in August had either materialised or were building. Those risks included a broader Middle East conflict pushing oil prices higher, cost pressures from the global AI boom, and tighter domestic capacity than assumed. Members said excess demand in the economy appeared greater than previously assessed. Staff increasingly questioned whether the unemployment rate consistent with target inflation was higher than thought, and business surveys pointed to a drift higher in firms’ inflation expectations.

The board also noted that, if global neutral interest rates have risen, the previous 4.35% cash rate was less restrictive than it had been two years earlier. It said holding steady while other central banks tightened could loosen Australian financial conditions through a weaker currency. Members concluded that they would remain attentive to incoming data and would raise rates further if required.

The third-quarter CPI report, due on 28 October at 00:30 GMT (20:30 ET on 27 October), now looks pivotal. The RBA’s next decision follows on 3 November at 03:30 GMT (22:30 ET on 2 November), alongside its updated quarterly forecasts. A strong reading on underlying and services inflation would test Goldman’s hold call and could push the board toward a second consecutive increase. 

---

item.title: Australia’s biggest planned IPO in 30 years pulled as AI infrastructure appetite cools
item.description:
The pullback in listings is a warning sign for the most capital-hungry corner of the AI trade. Developers that depend on fresh equity and debt to build face higher funding costs and tougher scrutiny of their pipelines. That is most negative for neocloud firms and newer developers without completed projects, which already showed in a weeklong slide in CoreWeave and Nebius. Established operators and chipmakers with proven demand are less exposed, but memory-chip weakness shows sentiment is fragile. Higher Treasury yields, driven partly by energy-led inflation, are the macro thread running through it, so a softer inflation backdrop would help reopen the window. Investors reserving capital for the Anthropic and OpenAI listings could also crowd out smaller deals in the coming months.

---

Earlier, hopes still up:

  • UBS sees 28% Q3 S&P 500 earnings growth, says AI and cyclicals can lift US stocks

---- The AI trade still has the market’s money, but data centre developers asking for it at listing are finding investors far more selective than a few months ago.

Summary:

  • ICYMI, Firmus Grid cancelled its Australian IPO, which at almost $5 billion would have been the country’s largest in 30 years, citing market volatility, and plans to raise funds privately and list in the US next year
  • AirTrunk, which had been preparing to list in Singapore, now hopes to go public in the first half of next year, The Wall Street Journal (gated) reported
  • Rising interest rates, a volatile market and political pushback against data centres are making investors warier, especially of developers with little track record
  • SoftBank’s SB Energy delayed its IPO after pushback on valuation; some investors are reserving capital for Anthropic’s planned listing
  • London-based Nscale is still aiming to list in the coming weeks, while Lambda has opened a final $4 billion pre-IPO round ahead of a planned listing next year

Australia’s Firmus Grid has cancelled what would have been the country’s largest initial public offering in 30 years, as rising interest rates, market volatility and political pushback cool investor appetite for AI data centre listings, The Wall Street Journal reported.

Firmus, which has close ties to Nvidia and is backed by Coatue and Blackstone, had planned to raise almost $5 billion. The company cited recent market volatility and prevailing conditions in pulling the deal and now plans to raise money privately and list on a US exchange next year, according to a person familiar with the matter. Within days, AirTrunk, another Blackstone-backed data centre operator that had been preparing to list in Singapore, pushed its plans back to the first half of next year amid concerns over volatility and interest rates.

The setbacks mark a sharp shift from just a few months ago, when investors were eager for almost any AI-linked listing. Companies that had targeted fourth-quarter debuts are now reconsidering their timing. Sentiment in parts of the AI trade has also turned fragile. Memory-chip makers from Micron to Samsung sold off on Tuesday on concerns about new competition from China, while neocloud firms CoreWeave and Nebius extended a weeklong decline.

Industry concerns were on display at a data centre conference in Las Vegas last week, where one panel was titled “Are We Screwed?” Attendees warned that market conditions and local opposition to data centres could tighten funding and derail deals. Bankers said the backlash is leading buyers to see infrastructure companies as riskier, giving sellers less credit for projects not yet built, with investors increasingly wary of developers lacking a record of completing projects.

That scrutiny has hit SoftBank’s SB Energy, which delayed its IPO after pushback on its potential valuation. Its filing showed it has no data centres in operation, despite a 10-gigawatt project in Ohio for OpenAI and a contracted backlog of more than $400 billion.

Investors are also becoming more selective, with some reserving capital for Anthropic’s planned offering later this year, the Journal reported. The planned listings of Anthropic and OpenAI, expected to be among the largest in market history, have both shaped and been shaped by the uncertainty. Anthropic is hosting an investor day at its San Francisco headquarters on Wednesday after pushing its timeline back by several weeks. Weak performance by recent IPOs is adding to the caution.

Some companies are pressing ahead. London-based Nscale is aiming to list in the coming weeks, though people familiar with its thinking acknowledged the timing is not ideal. Lambda, backed by Nvidia, Blackstone and Coatue, has opened a final $4 billion pre-IPO funding round ahead of a planned listing next year. Whether the window reopens is likely to depend on the path of interest rates and how the AI trade holds up through earnings season.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Trump says Taiwan to buy 30% of Alaska pipeline gas, again predicts lower oil prices
item.description:
Oil’s reaction to Trump’s repeated price forecasts has faded. The market’s own verdict shows in deferred contracts, where WTI and Brent strips for 2027 have recently set records, a sign that traders are pricing a lasting supply squeeze, not a swift resolution. The Alaska deals matter more for gas than oil. Asian buyers locking in North American supply away from the Gulf supports the case for diversification, but the volumes are years away and do nothing for this winter’s tight LNG market. A credible ceasefire would still trigger a sharp drop in crude, so headline risk cuts both ways, but traders are likely to need concrete steps, not statements, before pricing it.

---

Trump brought Asian money to Alaska LNG, but his latest promise of cheaper oil and a swift end to the Iran war meets a market that has heard it before, over, and over, and over again.

Summary:

  • Trump said Taiwan has agreed to buy 30% of the gas from the Alaska LNG pipeline project and invest around $4.4 billion, on top of South Korea’s $50 billion commitment
  • Speaking at a rally in Alaska, he said every permit needed for the project has been granted and that two deals would be announced
  • Trump said oil prices will fall soon and energy prices will drop sharply once the Iran war ends, which he said will happen very soon
  • He said Iran will not possess nuclear weapons and that more oil is being moved out of the Strait of Hormuz than before the war
  • Brent settled near $106 on Tuesday amid escalating Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, and Trump has made similar predictions repeatedly during the conflict

US President Donald Trump said Taiwan has agreed to buy 30% of the gas from the Alaska LNG pipeline project and invest around $4.4 billion in it, as he again predicted that oil prices would fall soon and that the war with Iran would end very soon.

Speaking at a rally in Alaska, Trump said every permit needed for the project has been granted and that two deals would be announced. Taiwan’s commitment adds to the $50 billion South Korea has pledged to invest, giving the long-planned project significant backing from Asian energy importers looking to diversify supply.

Trump also said energy prices would drop sharply as soon as the war ends and that Iran will not be allowed to possess nuclear weapons. He added that more oil is now being moved out of the Strait of Hormuz than before the conflict.

The comments are supportive on their face, but markets may treat them with some caution. Trump has repeatedly said during the conflict that the war would end soon and that oil prices would come down, and so far those forecasts have not materialised. Brent settled near $106 a barrel on Tuesday, while the conflict has widened, with Yemen’s Houthis stepping up missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia and loud explosions reported near Saudi Aramco’s headquarters in Dhahran.

His Hormuz claim is also more upbeat than some outside assessments. Morgan Stanley said recently that Persian Gulf crude exports had recovered to within 10% of prewar levels, a strong rebound but still short of where they were before the war.

The Alaska deals carry longer-term significance. Securing anchor buyers and investment from Taiwan and South Korea strengthens the commercial case for a project intended to send Alaskan gas to Asian markets, reducing their dependence on supply routes through the Gulf. However, a pipeline and export project of this scale would take years to deliver gas, offering no relief to current market tightness.

For oil traders, the test is whether the Iran conflict moves toward a concrete resolution. Until then, the market is likely to keep pricing the risk of further disruption over the promise of a quick end.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: How Singapore’s monetary policy works: the S$NEER band explained in three levers
item.description:
How Singapore’s monetary policy works: the S$NEER band explained in three levers

Most central banks fight inflation by raising or cutting interest rates. Singapore does it differently. The Monetary Authority of Singapore steers the economy by managing the value of the Singapore dollar against a basket of its trading partners’ currencies. When MAS “tightens,” it lets the currency strengthen faster, which makes imports cheaper and cools inflation. When it “eases,” it slows or reverses that appreciation.

That is why Wednesday’s decision to hold policy steady was framed entirely in terms of an exchange rate band, with no mention of an interest rate.

Why Singapore uses the exchange rate

Singapore is one of the most open economies in the world. It imports most of what it consumes, from food and fuel to raw materials, and trade flows are large relative to the size of its economy. That makes the exchange rate a far more powerful influence on prices than domestic interest rates.

There is also a practical constraint. Singapore allows capital to move freely in and out of the country. A central bank with open capital flows can control either its exchange rate or its interest rates, but not both. MAS chose the exchange rate in 1981, and local interest rates largely follow global rates, particularly those in the US.

What is the S$NEER?

The S$NEER, or Singapore dollar nominal effective exchange rate, measures the Singapore dollar against a weighted basket of the currencies of Singapore's main trading partners. MAS does not publish the basket's composition or weights. It manages the S$NEER within a policy band, stepping into the currency market when needed to keep it there.

The three levers

MAS adjusts policy through three features of the band, none of which it discloses precisely.

  • Slope: the speed of appreciation. The band is set on a gradual path, usually an upward one. A steeper slope means the Singapore dollar is allowed to strengthen faster, which is a tightening. A flatter slope is an easing. On Wednesday, MAS kept the slope unchanged.
  • Centre: the starting level. MAS can shift the midpoint of the band up or down in one step, known as re-centring. Moving the centre higher delivers an immediate, one-off strengthening, a stronger tightening signal than steepening the slope. MAS left the centre unchanged on Wednesday.
  • Width: how much movement is tolerated. A wider band gives the currency more room to fluctuate, usually used in periods of market volatility. A narrower band signals tighter control. The width was also unchanged.

Analysts estimate the band’s width and slope from the currency’s movements, but MAS keeps the exact parameters private. That gives it room to act without inviting speculation against fixed levels.

How often MAS decides

MAS reviews policy four times a year, in January, April, July and October, having moved from a twice-yearly schedule in 2024. Decisions are released early in the Singapore morning, which is around midnight GMT.

The inflation measure that matters

MAS focuses on core inflation, which excludes accommodation and private transport costs. Those categories are heavily influenced by government policy and housing and car-ownership cycles, so stripping them out gives a cleaner read on underlying price pressures. On Wednesday, MAS forecast core inflation to average 1.5% to 2.0% for 2026 and to ease more discernibly from mid-2027.

What Wednesday’s decision means

By leaving all three levers unchanged, MAS kept the Singapore dollar on its existing appreciating path. That is still a restraint on imported inflation, just not an increased one. All 10 analysts polled by Reuters had expected a tightening, most likely through a steeper slope, so the hold was a dovish surprise relative to expectations, even though the policy setting itself remains a tightening bias.

Key takeaway for traders

When reading an MAS statement, watch for the words “slope,” “width” and “centre.” Any change to them is the policy decision. For the Singapore dollar, the slope sets the medium-term direction against the basket, while a re-centring can produce a sharp immediate move. Because Singapore’s inflation is so sensitive to import costs, especially energy, oil prices are often a better guide to the next MAS move than local interest rates.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

  • Goldman Sachs says yuan undervalued by up to 25% and markets underestimate how far it can rise
China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day’s closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point. A stronger-than-expected CNY midpoint is typically read as a sign the PBOC is leaning against depreciation pressure, while a weaker fixing for the CNY can indicate tolerance for a softer currency, often in response to dollar strength or domestic economic headwinds.In periods of heightened global volatility, such as shifts in US rate expectations, trade tensions or capital flow pressures, the fixing takes on added significance. For investors, it provides insight into Beijing’s currency priorities, balancing competitiveness, capital stability and financial market confidence.

item.title: Saylor sees Bitcoin above $100,000, says investors will seek (scarce) assets that robots can’t make
item.description:
Friday’s upcoming MSCI decision on whether to exclude companies like Strategy from its global indices is the nearest catalyst, since an exclusion could trigger passive selling of the shares even if Saylor plays down its importance. Strategy’s new willingness to sell Bitcoin as well as buy it removes the assumption that the largest corporate holder is a one-way buyer, adding a potential source of supply in weaker markets. On the positive side, regulatory guidance from US agencies has eased a key overhang. Bitcoin still has to compete for capital with AI stocks and with Treasury yields that have risen sharply this year, so a turn lower in yields after US inflation data would be the clearest macro tailwind for his $100,000 call.

---

Saylor is talking his book, but his core pitch, that AI makes scarcity more valuable, is an argument worth weighing on its merits.

Summary:

  • Strategy executive chairman Michael Saylor said Bitcoin should move back above $100,000 after bottoming slightly below $60,000, with prices now in the $80,000s, but gave no timeframe
  • He argued AI will erode the value of labour-based equities and push investors towards scarce assets such as gold, prime real estate and Bitcoin
  • Saylor cited favourable US regulatory guidance, accelerating bank adoption and tokenisation as new tailwinds, calling the stalling of the Clarity Act good for the industry
  • He defended Strategy’s recent Bitcoin sales as part of running a structured finance company, but said the firm expects to keep adding to its holdings
  • Saylor called MSCI’s possible exclusion of Strategy from its indices, due to be decided on Friday, a bad precedent but said it was not that important to the company

Strategy co-founder and executive chairman Michael Saylor said Bitcoin is entering a new bull market and should climb back above $100,000, arguing that artificial intelligence will push investors towards assets whose supply cannot be expanded.

Speaking to Bloomberg Television at DC Fintech Week on Tuesday, Saylor said Bitcoin bottomed slightly below $60,000 during the past year’s contraction and has since rebounded into the $80,000s. He declined to give a timeframe for his $100,000 target, saying he plans in centuries, not months. Strategy’s longer-term forecast is for Bitcoin to grow 20% to 30% a year over the next two decades.

At the heart of his case is scarcity. Saylor argued that AI will reduce the value of companies built on large human workforces or on chasing the next breakthrough product, while increasing demand for scarce capital such as Palm Beach real estate, gold and Bitcoin. In his words, investors will look for things robots cannot make more of.

The argument has some logic. If AI makes labour and software abundant, assets with fixed supply could gain relative appeal. But it comes from the executive chairman of the world’s largest corporate Bitcoin holder, with a stake he put at more than $70 billion. Bloomberg’s interviewers also challenged it, noting that AI is absorbing much of the market’s capital and that the scarcity rotation has yet to show clearly in Bitcoin, which remains about 30% below last year’s record high.

Saylor countered that since Strategy began buying in August 2020, Bitcoin has returned about 38% a year and the company’s shares more than 50% a year, outpacing gold and every Magnificent Seven stock except Nvidia. By his own description, Bitcoin is also a volatile asset, with volatility of around 40, while Strategy’s shares run at roughly 80.

He pointed to new tailwinds: favourable US regulation, faster bank adoption, the spread of tokenised securities and the growth of digital credit. He said the Senate’s failure to advance the Clarity Act was the best outcome for the industry, as guidance from the Treasury, the SEC and the CFTC proved more supportive than the bill’s restrictions.

Saylor also defended Strategy’s sale of a small amount of Bitcoin in June, when prices were around $73,000, a move that unsettled the market. He described the company as a structured finance business that must be able to buy or sell Bitcoin, equity or credit as conditions require, mainly to support dividends on its credit products. He said those products pay 10% to 12% treated as a return of capital, which defers tax, and that the company expects to keep increasing its Bitcoin holdings in a bull market.

MSCI is due to decide on Friday whether to exclude companies like Strategy from its global indices on the grounds they mainly accumulate assets. Saylor called the proposal a bad precedent, argued Strategy is an operating company like banks and insurers, and said the decision was not that important to the firm. 

Explainer: MSCI, Strategy and the index question

What is MSCI? MSCI is one of the world’s largest index providers. Its benchmarks, such as the MSCI World and MSCI USA, are tracked by trillions of dollars in pension funds, ETFs and other investment products. When a company joins or leaves an MSCI index, funds that track it generally have to buy or sell the shares, whatever their view of the company.

What is Strategy? Strategy, formerly MicroStrategy and listed under the ticker MSTR, started as an enterprise software company. Since August 2020 it has focused on buying and holding Bitcoin, funded largely by issuing shares, debt and preferred-style securities. It is now the largest corporate holder of Bitcoin, with holdings Saylor puts at more than $70 billion.

What are “digital credit” products? These are Strategy’s income-paying securities, such as STRC, backed by the company’s Bitcoin holdings. Saylor says they pay 10% to 12% a year, treated as a return of capital, which generally defers tax rather than removing it. The company may sell Bitcoin or other assets to fund these payments, which is why it now says it must be free to sell as well as buy.

What is MSCI considering? MSCI has been reviewing whether companies whose main activity is accumulating digital assets, often called digital asset treasury companies, should stay in its global equity indices. It is assessing whether these firms are operating businesses or are closer to investment vehicles, which index providers often exclude.

Why does it matter? Exclusion could force index-tracking funds to sell Strategy shares, putting pressure on the stock and potentially on the company’s ability to raise money. It would also set a precedent for the growing number of similar companies. Saylor argues Strategy is an operating company comparable to banks and insurers, since it creates and sells credit products. He says the decision is not that important to the firm.

What happens next? MSCI is due to announce its decision on Friday, October 16. A decision to exclude would typically take effect at a later index review, giving funds time to adjust.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Singapore’s MAS holds policy steady, surprising all 10 analysts who expected tightening
item.description:
The decision is a dovish surprise against a unanimous call for tightening, which leaves the Singapore dollar vulnerable to some softening against its trading partners as positions built for a hawkish move unwind. The policy band still has an appreciating slope, though, so this is a pause in tightening, not an easing. Energy is the key swing factor. MAS explicitly flagged a sharp, sustained surge in energy prices as an upside risk, so a renewed jump in crude tied to Gulf escalation would put tightening firmly back on the table at the next review. Singapore’s position as a regional oil-trading and refining hub makes its imported inflation particularly sensitive to oil and refined product prices.

--

MAS chose patience over pre-emption, betting that slightly elevated inflation will ease on its own as the AI boom cools and import costs fade.

Summary:

  • The Monetary Authority of Singapore kept the rate of appreciation, width and centre of its S$NEER policy band unchanged
  • All 10 analysts polled by Reuters had expected MAS to tighten
  • MAS sees the economy expanding at a firm pace in the near term, then moderating as the AI cycle eases from its exceptional pace and global financial conditions tighten
  • Core inflation is forecast to average 1.5% to 2.0% in 2026, stay slightly elevated in the coming quarters and ease more discernibly from mid-2027
  • MAS said risks to inflation remain tilted to the upside, citing the potential for a sharp, sustained surge in energy or food prices

The Monetary Authority of Singapore kept its monetary policy settings unchanged on Wednesday, defying expectations for a tightening as it judged that slightly elevated inflation should ease over time.

The central bank, which manages policy through the exchange rate, said it would maintain the current rate of appreciation of its policy band, known as the Singapore dollar nominal effective exchange rate or S$NEER. There will be no change to the width of the band or the level at which it is centred. The band is already on an appreciating path, which helps restrain imported inflation, so the decision leaves that tightening bias in place without adding to it. All 10 analysts polled by Reuters had expected MAS to tighten.

MAS said the economy should continue to expand at a firm pace in the immediate quarters ahead, but moderate thereafter as the AI cycle eases from its exceptional pace and global financial conditions tighten. It expects AI-related activity to slow in the second half of 2027 and the economy’s positive output gap, a sign that demand is running ahead of capacity, to narrow through next year. The government will announce its growth forecasts for 2026 and 2027 in November.

On prices, MAS expects firming imported cost pressures to keep both core and headline inflation at their current slightly elevated levels in the months ahead. Core inflation is forecast to average 1.5% to 2.0% for 2026 as a whole, before easing more discernibly from the middle of next year as import costs ebb.

The central bank stressed that significant uncertainty surrounds the outlook and that, for now, risks to inflation remain tilted to the upside. A sharp and sustained surge in global energy or food prices could lift Singapore’s import costs by more than forecast. On the other hand, a larger-than-expected rise in interest rates or a sharper pullback in AI-related investment could drag on growth and, in turn, inflation.

The hold suggests MAS is prepared to look through near-term price pressures on the view that they will fade, while keeping its appreciating policy stance in place. With risks still skewed to the upside, the path of energy prices and the strength of the AI cycle are likely to shape whether it moves at its next review.

The Monetary Authority of Singapore is the coutnry's central bank.

In Europe, the strong inverse link between equities and Bund yields means an energy-driven inflation scare would hit stocks and bonds together, so gas storage heading into winter matters as much as the oil price for European equities. The French-German bond spread is set to remain a barometer of euro-area political risk into next year’s presidential election, with the potential to weigh on the euro and French banks. Oil and gas remain the key swing factors for whether Europe’s discount narrows.

---

Goldman’s Wilson sees investors who have cut risk to the bone facing a market where earnings are still growing fast and valuations have already come down.

Summary:

  • Mark Wilson, head of European equities franchise sales and hedge fund coverage at Goldman Sachs, favours long US megacap tech and a basket of German fiscal spending beneficiaries
  • He said Europe is more vulnerable than the US to the energy shock, with European stocks and 10-year Bund yields more negatively correlated than at any time since the 1990s
  • Hedge fund net equity exposure has been cut to multi-year lows in response to higher rates and other uncertainties
  • Wilson sees US third-quarter earnings growth of around 27%, likely the peak, with Europe growing around 22% in the second half, or 15% excluding energy
  • Clients are focused on the French-German bond yield spread and European gas inventories heading into winter
  • He is watching US CPI, a possible break in the Iran conflict before the US midterms, and third-quarter earnings

Goldman Sachs’ Mark Wilson favours US megacap technology stocks and German companies set to benefit from fiscal spending, arguing that strong earnings growth and lower valuations leave a constructive setup despite higher bond yields and energy prices.

Wilson, head of European equities franchise sales and hedge fund coverage at Goldman Sachs, said in an interview published by the bank that Europe is more vulnerable than the US to the energy shock, given greater inflationary pressure. On a six-month basis, European stocks and 10-year German Bund yields are around minus 70% correlated, a degree of inverse correlation not seen since the 1990s, which he described as a regime shift. Natural gas is as much of a concern as oil for Europe, he said, and clients are closely watching gas inventories as winter approaches.

Clients are also focused on France, where the spread between French and German government bond yields has widened sharply over political tensions around the budget. Wilson expects the issue to remain a feature of markets in the months ahead of the French presidential election in the first half of next year.

Higher rates have driven a logical de-rating of equities on both sides of the Atlantic, Wilson said, with rate-sensitive sectors such as European renewables down by more than 20%. Investors have cut risk sharply. Net exposure among US fundamental long-short hedge funds sits near the bottom of its one-year range and in the lowest few percent of its three- and five-year ranges, while global funds are in the bottom tenth of their ranges.

Wilson rejected the view that Europe is a value trap. He acknowledged that higher energy costs are a real competitive headwind showing up in company numbers, but said Europe already trades at a discount, partly reflecting that, and has kept pace with the US this year. He pointed to investment themes in rearmament, energy independence and industrials, and said AI deployment could ease the drag from Europe’s demographics. European banks, he noted, have outperformed the largest US tech stocks over one, three and four years.

On earnings, Wilson expects US third-quarter growth of around 27% (UBS is at 28%), probably the peak for this cycle, while Goldman forecasts European earnings growth of about 22% in the second half, or 15% excluding energy companies. Although growth is slowing at the margin, he said high nominal growth combined with compressed valuations keeps the setup favourable.

His first trade is long US megacap tech. He argued that hyperscaler revenue growth lags heavy capital spending by several quarters and that returns on that spending are beginning to come through. His second is long German fiscal spending beneficiaries. German manufacturing surveys are outpacing the US, earnings estimates for the group have risen by around 13% to 14% this year, yet the stocks have de-rated by more than 20% and trade on low-teens multiples.

Looking ahead, Wilson flagged US CPI as key to whether yields can stop rising. He also sees a window for a break in the Iran conflict ahead of the US midterm elections, with third-quarter earnings set to shape views on the AI trade.

  • AI-related spending is estimated to rise more than 80% this year to around $900 billion, and UBS expects semiconductors to account for about half of S&P 500 earnings growth in the quarter

UBS expects a strong third-quarter earnings season to give US equities room to climb, arguing that artificial intelligence spending, healthy cyclical demand and resilient consumers outweigh the drag from high energy prices.

The bank forecasts earnings per share growth of around 28% for S&P 500 companies in the September quarter. Its view comes after a cautious start to the week, when technology shares led US stocks lower and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell almost 3% as investors waited for inflation data and earnings, with elevated oil prices and geopolitical conflict also weighing on sentiment.

AI remains the main driver of profits, according to UBS. It estimates AI-related spending will rise by more than 80% this year to around $900 billion and expects semiconductor companies alone to deliver about half of S&P 500 earnings growth in the quarter. Although capital spending growth is forecast to slow next year, UBS said the investment appears to be paying off for the large cloud providers known as hyperscalers. It expects their cloud revenue to grow by close to 60% year on year in the quarter, accelerating from just under 50% in the June quarter, with consumer AI agents seen as the next source of demand.

UBS also expects profit growth to broaden beyond technology. The new orders component of the ISM manufacturing index has stayed in expansion for nine straight months, and the bank noted that such stretches have historically lasted about three years on average. That suggests further room for growth among manufacturers and sectors such as industrials.

Consumers should hold up, in UBS’s view. Higher energy costs may squeeze spending at the lower end, but with initial jobless claims near multi-decade lows, the bank expects labour market strength to prevent a meaningful slowdown in overall spending.

UBS acknowledged that higher energy prices are a headwind, particularly for retailers and goods manufacturers exposed to freight costs. Travel-related companies are already feeling the impact, and manufacturers may face higher input prices. However, the bank sees only a limited effect on aggregate index profits.

Rising borrowing costs are also manageable, according to UBS. The 10-year Treasury yield has climbed by more than one percentage point this year, but non-financial S&P 500 companies have a weighted average debt maturity of about 11 years, meaning little of their debt is resetting to higher rates. UBS expects volatility to persist but sees scope for US stocks to move higher on the back of still-strong profit growth.
